body.heading: Keep it small and scheduled
paragraphs: A family meeting works when it is boring in structure: same time most weeks, twenty minutes, one small list. Scheduling it removes the drama of calling one — nobody has to guess whether this conversation means catastrophe.
Start with what went well. It sounds soft; it is actually structural. Meetings that open with gratitude get through the difficult items with measurably less shouting.

body.heading: One speaker, one topic
paragraphs: Two rules carry the whole thing: one person speaks at a time, and each item gets finished before the next begins. Most family arguments are actually three arguments braided together; unbraiding them is nine-tenths of the solution.
Young children can hold a talking object; adults, in our experience, sometimes need one too.

body.heading: End with decisions, not victories
paragraphs: Close each item with who does what by when, said out loud and agreed. Unfinished items go on next week’s list without shame. A family meeting is not a court; nobody should leave with a verdict, only with a plan.
And end on time, even mid-success. Leaving people wanting slightly more meeting is the secret to them attending the next one.

takeaway: Same time, short list, one topic at a time, and decisions instead of verdicts.
